title: Inclusive Design
author: Catherine Baker
source: FFT Tutoring with the Lightning Squad (tutoring.fft.org.uk), screenshots supplied 6 Oct 2026

pages.heading: An Accessible World
pages.text: Wouldn’t it be nice to live in a world where everyone could move around easily, and get to wherever they needed to go, with minimum fuss and maximum enjoyment? Well, nowadays many designers are working on making that happen! Every single building you go into has been designed by someone. So has every object you use in your daily life, from a paperclip to a mobile phone to a bathroom basin. Designers have to make a huge number of decisions when they are designing objects and buildings. One of the main things they have to think about is accessibility. Accessible buildings and objects are those that can be used by anyone, regardless of their age, ability or circumstances.

pages.heading: Design in the Past
pages.text: In the past, most buildings and public spaces were designed without much thought for people who might have limited mobility. Buildings like schools, hospitals and libraries were often constructed with long flights of stairs. This made it very difficult for people who used wheelchairs or other mobility aids to even get inside them! People trying to go places with young children in pushchairs would often find access difficult too.

pages.heading: Excluded
pages.text: If they did manage to get through the door of a building, people with limited mobility might well struggle to move around inside it, especially if they needed to go upstairs. Corridors and other indoor spaces might be too narrow or cluttered to navigate in a wheelchair, making life even harder. Quite often, essential facilities like toilets would be inaccessible to people using wheelchairs. Because of the way that the buildings were designed, people with limited mobility were effectively excluded from a lot of public spaces. This meant it was harder for them to take part in the important things that many of us take for granted – from jobs, education and shopping to hobbies and entertainment.

pages.heading: What is Inclusive Design?
pages.text: Today, designers give a lot of thought to ensuring that the buildings and objects they create can be used by everybody, including people with limited mobility, deaf people and people with visual impairments. This kind of design, aimed at making things equally accessible for everyone, is often called inclusive or universal design.

pages.heading: Ramps and Automatic Doors
pages.text: There are lots of ways to use inclusive design when creating buildings and public spaces. For example, imagine an old-fashioned building with a flight of stairs leading up to a heavy wooden door that must be opened by hand with a stiff handle. It would be incredibly difficult for someone using a wheelchair to get into that building unaided. However, instead of the stairs, a designer could create a beautiful curving ramp, which is as easy to use in a wheelchair as on foot. The heavy door could be replaced with an automatic door, which opens whenever someone approaches it. Inside, the building could feature a central lift that gives access to all floors in the building so people don’t have to climb stairs.

pages.heading: Accessible Streets
pages.text: Think of an old-fashioned street, with high kerbs, cracks and lumps in the pavement. That would be difficult and uncomfortable to travel along in a wheelchair, and it might not be easy to get across the kerb if you wanted to cross the road. If the pavements were designed to be smooth and level with the road surface, it would be far easier for wheelchair users to get around. At road crossings, sounds could be used as well as lights to let people know when it is safe to cross the road. That way, everyone could use the crossing, including visually impaired and deaf people. A lot of these design features are already very common in modern buildings and public spaces but inclusive design doesn’t stop there!

pages.heading: At Home
pages.text: There are lots of inclusive design features that can help everyone to live comfortably at home. Some people find it difficult to make particular movements, such as twisting a tap or reaching up to switch a light on or off. Designers can create taps that are motion activated, which are easier to turn off and on. Light switches can be installed at any height or they could be replaced entirely! These days, it’s possible to get voice-activated lights which don’t need to be physically turned on or off at all. Lights, heating and many home appliances can also be controlled via smartphone apps – which means people can easily turn them on and off without having to move.

pages.heading: In the Bathroom
pages.text: The bathroom is another place where inclusive design can help. Bathrooms are potentially dangerous places for anyone, with wet surfaces that make it easy to slip and fall. A grab rail is handy because you can hold on to it to steady you when you use the toilet or get into or out of the bath or shower. This can help everyone, including people with limited mobility. People who can’t bend to get in and out of the bath might have a special bath seat fitted to lower them into the water. Some baths and showers have been designed to make it easy to just walk into them and sit down, without any need to step over a high bath edge. That means that anyone can have a comfortable bath or shower, including people with limited mobility.

pages.heading: In the Kitchen
pages.text: There are lots of ways to make the kitchen accessible for everyone, too. For example, you can have work surfaces at varying heights, so that both people who use wheelchairs and people who don’t can easily reach everything they need to cook a meal. Some people, for example those with sensory autism, find the noise of kitchen appliances such as washing machines to be overwhelming, but these days, quieter models are available. Quieter washing machines are an example of inclusive design, because they make washing clothes a more pleasant experience for everyone.

pages.heading: Modern Technology
pages.text: Modern technology provides some brilliant opportunities for inclusive design. These days, it’s not just lights that can be voice activated! Voice activated smartphones and home speakers also exist. These help people to make and receive calls and text messages, listen to audio books and podcasts, set reminders and do all kinds of things online, all without needing to hold or look at the phone. It’s obvious how this might be helpful to people who are visually impaired, but anyone might find a voice activated phone useful if their phone is out of reach, or if they’re busy doing something and can’t pick up the phone.

pages.heading: Working from Home
pages.text: Since the COVID-19 pandemic, there has been a big rise in working from home, aided by technology such as video calls and instant messaging. This has brought benefits for many people, including people with limited mobility. Working from home often means being able to work flexibly, at times to suit the worker, and in a comfortable environment. It also means the worker avoids having to go through a daily commute, which can be particularly challenging for people with limited mobility.

pages.heading: Inclusive Play
pages.text: Inclusive design ideas can help everyone have fun, too! For example, swimming is a great hobby that’s also extremely good for you. However, some people have been unable to take part in swimming because they don’t have the mobility to get into the swimming pool – even though they can swim quite easily once in the water. Special chair lifts fixed to the side of the pool, allow people with limited mobility to easily enter the water, and get out whenever they want to.

pages.heading: Inclusive Sport
pages.text: Many sports can be made more accessible for people with particular needs. Sometimes it’s as simple as ensuring that sports grounds, changing rooms and other facilities are fully accessible for people with limited mobility. Maybe more space is needed around gym equipment, so users in wheelchairs can access the equipment easily. Sometimes there are other things that can be done – for example, wheelchair users may find it hard to play some sports on a grass field, so a hard surfaced playing field might work better for them. Outdoor play areas for children are also being made more accessible by ensuring that the equipment has step-free access so everyone can take part in the fun!

pages.heading: The Future of Inclusive Design
pages.text: We’ve come a long way with inclusive design, but there’s still much to do until all areas and aspects of life are fully accessible for everyone. This is something we all need to think about, because inclusive design makes life better for everyone, not just the differently abled. A world where everyone can move around safely and easily, and everyone can play a fulfilling part, is a better world for all of us. All of us can contribute to this. Do you have an idea that could help people access places and activities that are currently out of reach for them? If so, you could be part of the future of inclusive design!

glossary.accessible: Easy for everyone to get into, reach or use, whatever their age or ability.
glossary.mobility: How easily someone can move their body or get from place to place.
glossary.navigate: Find your way around a place.
glossary.facilities: Rooms or equipment provided for people to use, such as toilets or changing rooms.
glossary.excluded: Kept out; not able to join in.
glossary.appliances: Machines used at home, such as washing machines, kettles and fridges.
glossary.contribute: Give or add something to help.
